title: Hazel and Patch's Mystery Notes
markdown:
The house sat snug against a meadow that stayed green even when the laundry on the line had given up. Inside, in the toy box that smelled of wood and yesterday’s games, Hazel the squirrel kept her tail in a state of permanent suggestion. Her eyes had the flicker of something that wanted a farther room. Patch the teddy filled the rest of the box: worn fur, seams loved into softness, one good button eye that did the work of two. He was a mountain of quiet when quiet was required, and a mountain of caution when it was not.

Their days had a rhythm. Play until the human’s voice went bedtime-soft. Stories told in the hush that comes after teeth are brushed. Sleep that arrived on schedule. Hazel liked the rhythm and, at the same time, felt a burr under it — the wild strip of world past the garden, where hazel bushes tangled and mushrooms kept their own hours, wide caps like little stages.

Every day was the comfortable version of that. Predictable. Kind. Slightly too small.

Until the notes.

They appeared on the mushroom caps at the garden’s edge, right where the wild hazel began its tangled dance, folded as small as a secret and polite to the point of apology. Apologies for any disturbance. Hoping the night air is agreeable. The garden’s usual chatter thinned into whispers. Someone, or something, was writing as if it were a guest in its own yard. The ink looked careful. The folds looked sorry.

Hazel’s expedition-heart started at once. She prodded Patch until his stuffing creaked and his button eye opened on the problem. “We have to find who.” Her voice was a delighted squeak. Her eyes had the shine of polished acorns. Patch considered the dark beyond the curtains. “It is awfully late. And the notes are… strange.” She was already a question mark of tail at the window, halfway to gone.

They went out as two determined shadows. The garden held its breath: damp earth, a sweet night-flower smell that needed no explorer’s swamp to be itself, a humidity that made the leaves look as if they were thinking. Their objective was the hazel copse, and Hazel named it under her breath as if naming made a map. She darted, a blur. Patch waddled, which was his pace and not a failing, and the grass combed his worn fur the wrong way.

A croak, deep enough to rearrange the stillness, sat them both back on their heels. Myfanwy the toad occupied a mossy stone as if it were a bench reserved for commentary. Her throat pulsed. Golden eyes took them in without hurry. “You are in motion,” she said, pebbles tumbling in the voice. “You are inspecting the fungi. The notes are located upon the fungi.”

Hazel began a theory — sprites, gnomes, a very tidy beetle. Myfanwy blinked. “Observation: the notes are present. You seek the originator. A logical hypothesis. Presently unproven.” Literalness, Hazel found, could be as odd as mystery, and harder to argue with.

They pressed into the copse. Moonlight sliced the floor into stripes. An arched wooden bridge took their weight in small complaints, planks rippling with moon-shadow. Near a stand of feathery ferns Hazel’s eye caught a pearly button, familiar as a habit she had accused the toy box of eating. “Mine.” Patch tilted his head. “I was sure I had lost that. Ages ago.”

Farther on, peeking from beneath a blackberry’s thorn, a loop of crimson ribbon. Patch’s fur prickled. “I looked for that all yesterday. It was my favourite.”

Hazel nosed a drift of fallen leaves that had no business being so neatly piled. A scrap of paper, crumpled, forgotten on purpose or by accident. So terribly sorry about the leaf mess, in a scrawl that made both of them go still. Myfanwy, who had followed with the patience of weather, croaked softly. “Observation: the penmanship resembles yours, Hazel. And yours, Patch.”

Not a sprite. Not a gnome with manners. Them. In the half-waking fuss of other nights they had written to themselves, or to each other, and let dawn take the memory. Hazel’s notes were jitters about going farther than the toy box, the itch she had not wanted to say aloud. Patch’s were the worry of being left when the going got interesting, the fear of a change of shape. Polite apologies for nerves they had not wanted to carry in daylight.

Hazel felt heat under her fur. “I do get carried away.” Patch folded his arms around himself, a hug with no one else required. “And I mind when the shape of things changes.” Myfanwy stated the remaining obvious with ambassadorial gravity — that paper was paper, that they were they — then seemed content to have done her job. She did not offer a moral. Toads, at least this one, left morals to people who enjoyed them.

They sat on the moon-striped bridge. The wood was cool through fur and felt. The air, which had been heavy with invented peril, tasted like ordinary night, clean after a held breath. They gathered the notes, the button, the ribbon. Hazel tucked the button into the same pocket as the ribbon, which was a kind of answer that did not require a speech. The mushrooms, empty now, looked like mushrooms again.

Ever since then they have still gone out when the house goes quiet. The copse still rustles. The mushrooms sometimes hold a new scrap, and sometimes they do not. Myfanwy continues to confirm that what is on a cap is on a cap. Hazel still runs ahead, but she glances back before the ferns close. Patch still worries, and then he comes anyway, the ribbon end showing like a small red fact against his worn chest, the button a hard comforting circle in the dark.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing night-time woodland adventure for older children
